learningObjectives: Place the Requirements and TestCase Design sections within the classic Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC).
Explain why Tosca separates 'what to test' (Requirements) from 'how the test data is structured' (TestCase Design).
Describe the Tricentis philosophy of investing more time up front in test design to reduce execution and regression effort later.
Preview the ten lessons that make up the Test Design Specialist Level 1 course.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Where TDS1 fits in the testing lifecycle

elements.description: This course prepares you to work in the two Tosca sections that sit at the front of the STLC: Requirements (colored yellow in Tosca Commander) and TestCase Design (colored red). Together they cover the analysis and planning phases — figuring out what needs to be tested and how much data variation is needed — before any physical TestCase is built.

Answers 'what needs to be tested and how risky is it if it breaks?'. Requirements are defined, structured, and risk-weighted so testers know where to focus first, and so progress can be tracked against them later.

Answers 'what data combinations do I need to prove each Requirement works?'. Business behavior and test data are translated into a structured, combinable format — the TestSheet — before a single physical TestCase is built in the TestCase section (which was covered in the Automation Specialist courses).

elements.title: The rest of the cycle (not the focus of this course)
items: Reporting back against the Requirements — closing the loop

bulletPoints: Requirements = yellow section, TestCase Design = red section, TestCase = blue section, in Tosca Commander's color scheme.
TDS1 covers the analysis + planning stages; building physical TestCases was covered in AS1/AS2.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Why invest time up front in test design

elements.description: On many projects, only a small fraction of testing time is spent specifying test cases (often done ad-hoc/intuitively), while the vast majority is spent in execution — and that execution effort repeats every regression cycle. Weak upfront design tends to produce redundant test cases that over-cover high-visibility requirements while under-covering others.

Shift more effort into the design phase: define Requirements, weight them by risk, and derive test data combinations systematically (covered across Lessons 1-10). The payoff is fewer but more precise test cases, each with a clear, isolated purpose — which also makes failures faster to diagnose, because a well-designed TestCase only fails for one reason.

elements.text: Linking TestCase Design back to Requirements (Lesson 7) turns the Requirements section into a live project dashboard — risk coverage, execution state, and outstanding work are all visible from one place.

bulletPoints: Goal: minimum number of TestCases for maximum, precise risk coverage — not maximum test cases.
A TestCase with a single clear focus is faster to debug when it fails.

elements.title: Lessons 1-10
items: Lesson 1 — Requirements: Folders, RequirementSets, Requirements, and risk weighting.
Lesson 2 — Attributes: structuring a TestSheet with Administration/Precondition/Process/Verification.
Lesson 4 — Combinatorial Methods: All Combinations, Orthogonal, Pairwise, and Linear Expansion.
Lesson 5 — TestCase Specifications: filling in TestSheet values efficiently.
Lesson 6 — Classes: reusing Attribute structures across TestSheets.
Lesson 7 — Link to Requirements: connecting TestCase Design back to the Requirements dashboard.
Lesson 8 — Integration of New Attributes: adapting a TestSheet when the SUT changes.
Lesson 9 — Best Practices: readability, reuse, and Agile (Given-When-Then) structuring.
Lesson 10 — Automatic Generation of Instances: letting Tosca generate combinations for you.

bulletPoints: The course uses Tricentis' sample DemoWebShop application for hands-on exercises.

examPitfalls.title: Treating TDS1 as an automation course
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming this course teaches how to build and execute automated TestSteps, like AS1/AS2 did.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: TDS1 is about analysis and planning — Requirements and TestCase Design (yellow and red sections). Building the physical, executable TestCase (blue section) was covered in the Automation Specialist courses.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing 'more test cases' with 'better coverage'
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming that generating as many TestCase combinations as possible is the goal of good test design.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The Tricentis methodology explicitly favors fewer, more precise TestCases with a clear individual focus over exhaustive combination counts — see the Combinatorial Methods lesson for how Linear Expansion achieves this.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which two Tosca Commander sections does the Test Design Specialist Level 1 course focus on?
practiceQuiz.hint: Think about the two phases that happen before a physical TestCase is ever built.
practiceQuiz.rationale: TDS1 covers Requirements (yellow) — defining and risk-weighting what needs to be tested — and TestCase Design (red) — structuring the test data combinations needed to prove those Requirements.

practiceQuiz.scenario: According to the Tricentis test design philosophy, what should happen when more time is invested in the TestCase Design phase?

options.text: Execution time increases proportionally, since more TestCases are created.
Execution and regression time should decrease, because TestCases are fewer, more precise, and non-redundant.
Nothing changes in execution; design time is purely additional overhead.

practiceQuiz.hint: The traditional problem was too much ad-hoc execution effort repeated every regression cycle — what does upfront design fix?
practiceQuiz.rationale: By front-loading effort into careful TestCase Design, testers avoid redundant coverage and produce precise, clearly-scoped TestCases — which reduces the time spent executing and re-executing tests during every regression cycle.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What allows the Requirements section to function as a live project dashboard?

options.text: Manually updating a spreadsheet alongside Tosca.
Linking TestCase Design, TestCases, and ExecutionLists back to the Requirements, so risk coverage and execution state roll up automatically.
Requirements are dashboards by default and require no linking.
Only the ExecutionList section can show project status.

practiceQuiz.hint: This is previewed here and covered in full in Lesson 7.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Once TestSheets, TestCases, and ExecutionLists are linked back to Requirements, the Requirements section aggregates coverage and execution state, giving a real-time view of project progress and remaining risk.
